cards.front:
**Security / No runtime code generation**

Explain No runtime code generation in the context of Security.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

Since native AOT generates all code at the time of publishing the app, no new executable code needs to be generated at runtime. This allows running your apps in environments that disallow creation of new executable code pages at runtime. All the code that the CPU executes can be digitally signed.

---
Adapted from [Microsoft and contributors](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/core/deploying/native-aot/security.md). [CC BY 4.0; code MIT](/licenses/library-dotnet--docs.txt). Prompts, formatting, and selected wording adapted for Recall; source license applies to this material.

cards.front:
**Security / Restricted reflection surface**

Explain Restricted reflection surface in the context of Security.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

When apps are published with native AOT, the compiler analyzes the usage of reflection within the app. Only the program elements that were deemed to be targets of reflection are available for reflection at runtime. Places within the program that attempt to do unconstrained reflection are flagged using [trimming warnings](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/core/deploying/trimming/fixing-warnings.md). Program elements that weren't intended to be targets of reflection cannot be reflected on. This restriction can prevent a class of issues where a malicious actor gets in control of what the program reflects on and invokes unintended code. This restriction includes approaches that use `Assembly.LoadFrom` or `Reflection.Emit` - neither of those work with native AOT, and their use is flagged with a warning at build time.

---
Adapted from [Microsoft and contributors](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/core/deploying/native-aot/security.md). [CC BY 4.0; code MIT](/licenses/library-dotnet--docs.txt). Prompts, formatting, and selected wording adapted for Recall; source license applies to this material.

cards.front:
**Compiler Options - security options / KeyFile**

Explain KeyFile in the context of Compiler Options - security options.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

Specifies the filename containing the cryptographic key.

```xml
<KeyFile>filename</KeyFile>
```

`file` is the name of the file containing the strong name key. When this option is used, the compiler inserts the public key from the specified file into the assembly manifest and then signs the final assembly with the private key. To generate a key file, type `sn -k file` at the command line. If you compile with [**-target:module**](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/output.md#outputtype), the name of the key file is held in the module and incorporated into the assembly created when you compile an assembly with [**AddModules**](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/inputs.md#addmodules). You can also pass your encryption information to the compiler with [**KeyContainer**](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/security.md#keycontainer). Use [**DelaySign**](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/security.md#delaysign) if you want a partially signed assembly. In case both **KeyFile** and **KeyContainer** are specified in the same compilation, the compiler will first try the key container. If that succeeds, then the assembly is signed with the information in the key container. If the compiler doesn't find the key container, it will try the file specified with [**KeyFile**](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/security.md#keyfile). If that succeeds, the assembly is signed with the information in the key file and the key information will be installed in the key container. On the next compilation, the key container will be valid. A key file might contain only the public key. For more information, see [Creating and Using Strong-Named Assemblies](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/standard/assembly/create-use-strong-named.md) and [Delay Signing an Assembly](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/standard/assembly/delay-sign.md).

---
Adapted from [Microsoft and contributors](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/security.md). [CC BY 4.0; code MIT](/licenses/library-dotnet--docs.txt). Prompts, formatting, and selected wording adapted for Recall; source license applies to this material.

cards.front:
**Compiler Options - security options / KeyContainer**

Explain KeyContainer in the context of Compiler Options - security options.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

Specifies the name of the cryptographic key container.

```xml
<KeyContainer>container</KeyContainer>
```

`container` is the name of the strong name key container. When the **KeyContainer** option is used, the compiler creates a sharable component. The compiler inserts a public key from the specified container into the assembly manifest and signs the final assembly with the private key. To generate a key file, type `sn -k file` at the command line. `sn -i` installs the key pair into a container. This option isn't supported when the compiler runs on CoreCLR. To sign an assembly when building on CoreCLR, use the [**KeyFile**](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/security.md#keyfile) option. If you compile with [**OutputType**](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/output.md#outputtype), the name of the key file is held in the module and incorporated into the assembly when you compile this module into an assembly with [**AddModules**](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/inputs.md#addmodules). You can also specify this option as a custom attribute (`System.Reflection.AssemblyKeyNameAttribute`) in the source code for any common intermediate language (CIL) module. You can also pass your encryption information to the compiler with [**KeyFile**](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/security.md#keyfile). Use [**DelaySign**](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/security.md#delaysign) to add the public key  to the assembly manifest but signing the assembly until it has been tested. For more information, see [Creating and Using Strong-Named Assemblies](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/standard/assembly/create-use-strong-named.md) and [Delay Signing an Assembly](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/standard/assembly/delay-sign.md).

---
Adapted from [Microsoft and contributors](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/security.md). [CC BY 4.0; code MIT](/licenses/library-dotnet--docs.txt). Prompts, formatting, and selected wording adapted for Recall; source license applies to this material.

cards.front:
**Compiler Options - security options / HighEntropyVA**

Explain HighEntropyVA in the context of Compiler Options - security options.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

The **HighEntropyVA** compiler option tells the Windows kernel whether a particular executable supports high entropy Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR).

```xml
<HighEntropyVA>true</HighEntropyVA>
```

This option specifies that a 64-bit executable or an executable that is marked by the [**PlatformTarget**](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/output.md#platformtarget) compiler option supports a high entropy virtual address space. The option is enabled by default for all .NET Standard and .NET Core versions, and .NET Framework versions starting with .NET Framework 4.5.

The **HighEntropyVA** option enables compatible versions of the Windows kernel to use higher degrees of entropy when randomizing the address space layout of a process as part of ASLR. Using higher degrees of entropy means a larger number of addresses can be allocated to memory regions such as stacks and heaps. As a result, it's more difficult to guess the location of a particular memory region. The **HighEntropyVA** compiler option requires the target executable and any modules that it depends on can handle pointer values larger than 4 gigabytes (GB) when they're running as a 64-bit process.

---
Adapted from [Microsoft and contributors](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-options/security.md). [CC BY 4.0; code MIT](/licenses/library-dotnet--docs.txt). Prompts, formatting, and selected wording adapted for Recall; source license applies to this material.

cards.front:
**Assembly security considerations / Overview**

Explain the key points of Assembly security considerations, including any stated conditions or limitations.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

When you build an assembly, you can specify a set of permissions that the assembly requires to run. Whether certain permissions are granted or not granted to an assembly is based on evidence.

There are two distinct ways evidence is used:

- The input evidence is merged with the evidence gathered by the loader to create a final set of evidence used for policy resolution. The methods that use this semantic include **Assembly.Load**, **Assembly.LoadFrom**, and **Activator.CreateInstance**.

- The input evidence is used unaltered as the final set of evidence used for policy resolution. The methods that use this semantic include **Assembly.Load(byte\[])** and **AppDomain.DefineDynamicAssembly()**.

  Optional permissions can be granted by the [security policy](https://github.com/previous-versions/dotnet/framework/code-access-security/code-access-security-basics) set on the computer where the assembly will run. If you want your code to handle all potential security exceptions, you can do one of the following:

- Insert a permission request for all the permissions your code must have, and handle up front the load-time failure that occurs if the permissions are not granted.

- Do not use a permission request to obtain permissions your code might need, but be prepared to handle security exceptions if permissions are not granted.

  > Security is a complex area, and you have many options to choose from. For more information, see [Key Security Concepts](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/standard/security/key-security-concepts.md).

At load time, the assembly's evidence is used as input to security policy. Security policy is established by the enterprise and the computer's administrator as well as by user policy settings, and determines the set of permissions that's granted to all managed code when executed. Security policy can be established for the publisher of the assembly (if it has a signing tool generated signature), for the Web site and zone (which was an Internet Explorer concept) that the assembly was downloaded from, or for the assembly's strong name. For example, a computer's administrator can establish security policy that allows all code downloaded from a Web site and signed by a given software company to access a database on a computer, but does not grant access to write to the computer's disk.

---
Adapted from [Microsoft and contributors](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/standard/assembly/security-considerations.md). [CC BY 4.0; code MIT](/licenses/library-dotnet--docs.txt). Prompts, formatting, and selected wording adapted for Recall; source license applies to this material.

cards.front:
**Assembly security considerations / Strong-named assemblies and signing tools**

Explain Strong-named assemblies and signing tools in the context of Assembly security considerations.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

> Do not rely on strong names for security. They provide a unique identity only.

You can sign an assembly in two different but complementary ways: with a strong name or by using  [SignTool.exe (Sign Tool)](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/framework/tools/signtool-exe.md). Signing an assembly with a strong name adds public key encryption to the file containing the assembly manifest. Strong name signing helps to verify name uniqueness, prevent name spoofing, and provide callers with some identity when a reference is resolved.

No level of trust is associated with a strong name, which makes [SignTool.exe (Sign Tool)](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/framework/tools/signtool-exe.md) important. The two signing tools require a publisher to prove its identity to a third-party authority and obtain a certificate. This certificate is then embedded in your file and can be used by an administrator to decide whether to trust the code's authenticity.

You can give both a strong name and a digital signature created using [SignTool.exe (Sign Tool)](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/framework/tools/signtool-exe.md) to an assembly, or you can use either alone. The two signing tools can sign only one file at a time; for a multifile assembly, you sign the file that contains the assembly manifest. A strong name is stored in the file containing the assembly manifest, but a signature created using [SignTool.exe (Sign Tool)](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/framework/tools/signtool-exe.md) is stored in a reserved slot in the portable executable (PE) file containing the assembly manifest. Signing of an assembly using [SignTool.exe (Sign Tool)](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/framework/tools/signtool-exe.md) can be used (with or without a strong name) when you already have a trust hierarchy that relies on [SignTool.exe (Sign Tool)](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/framework/tools/signtool-exe.md) generated signatures, or when your policy uses only the key portion and does not check a chain of trust.

> When using both a strong name and a signing tool signature on an assembly, the strong name must be assigned first.

The common language runtime also performs a hash verification; the assembly manifest contains a list of all files that make up the assembly, including a hash of each file as it existed when the manifest was built. As each file is loaded, its contents are hashed and compared with the hash value stored in the manifest. If the two hashes do not match, the assembly fails to load.

Strong naming and signing using [SignTool.exe (Sign Tool)](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/framework/tools/signtool-exe.md) guarantee integrity through digital signatures and certificates. All the technologies mentioned, that is, hash verification, strong naming, and signing using [SignTool.exe (Sign Tool)](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/framework/tools/signtool-exe.md), work together to ensure that the assembly has not been altered in any way.

---
Adapted from [Microsoft and contributors](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/standard/assembly/security-considerations.md). [CC BY 4.0; code MIT](/licenses/library-dotnet--docs.txt). Prompts, formatting, and selected wording adapted for Recall; source license applies to this material.

cards.front:
**XSLT Security Considerations / Overview**

Explain the key points of XSLT Security Considerations, including any stated conditions or limitations.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

The XSLT language has a rich set of features that give you a great deal of power and flexibility. It includes many features that, while useful, could also be exploited by outside sources. In order to use XSLT safely, you must understand the types of security issues that arise when using XSLT, and the basic strategies that you can employ to mitigate these risks.

---
Adapted from [Microsoft and contributors](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/standard/data/xml/xslt-security-considerations.md). cards.front:
**XSLT Security Considerations / XSLT Extensions**

Explain XSLT Extensions in the context of XSLT Security Considerations.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

Two popular XSLT extensions are style sheet scripting and extension objects. These extensions allow the XSLT processor to execute code.

- Extension objects add programming capabilities to XSL transformations.

- Scripts can be embedded in the style sheet using the `msxsl:script` extension element.

---
Adapted from [Microsoft and contributors](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/standard/data/xml/xslt-security-considerations.md). [CC BY 4.0; code MIT](/licenses/library-dotnet--docs.txt). Prompts, formatting, and selected wording adapted for Recall; source license applies to this material.

cards.front:
**XSLT Security Considerations / XSLT Extensions / Extension Objects**

Explain XSLT Extensions / Extension Objects in the context of XSLT Security Considerations.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

Extension objects are added using the `System.Xml.Xsl.XsltArgumentList.AddExtensionObject` method. The FullTrust permission set is required to support extension objects. This ensures that elevation of permissions does not happen when extension object code is executed. Attempting to call the `System.Xml.Xsl.XsltArgumentList.AddExtensionObject` method without FullTrust permissions results in a security exception being thrown.

---
Adapted from [Microsoft and contributors](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/standard/data/xml/xslt-security-considerations.md). [CC BY 4.0; code MIT](/licenses/library-dotnet--docs.txt). Prompts, formatting, and selected wording adapted for Recall; source license applies to this material.

cards.front:
**XSLT Security Considerations / XSLT Extensions / Style Sheet Scripts**

Explain XSLT Extensions / Style Sheet Scripts in the context of XSLT Security Considerations.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

Scripts can be embedded in a style sheet using the `msxsl:script` extension element. Script support is an optional feature on the `System.Xml.Xsl.XslCompiledTransform` class that is disabled by default. Scripting can be enabled by setting the `System.Xml.Xsl.XsltSettings.EnableScript` property to `true` and passing the `System.Xml.Xsl.XsltSettings` object to the `System.Xml.Xsl.XslCompiledTransform.Load` method.

> Script blocks are supported only in .NET Framework. They are *not* supported on .NET Core or .NET 5 or later.

---
Adapted from [Microsoft and contributors](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/standard/data/xml/xslt-security-considerations.md). [CC BY 4.0; code MIT](/licenses/library-dotnet--docs.txt). Prompts, formatting, and selected wording adapted for Recall; source license applies to this material.

cards.front:
**XSLT Security Considerations / XSLT Extensions / Style Sheet Scripts / Guidelines**

Explain XSLT Extensions / Style Sheet Scripts / Guidelines in the context of XSLT Security Considerations.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

Enable scripting only when the style sheet comes from a trusted source. If you cannot verify the source of the style sheet, or if the style sheet does not come from a trusted source, pass in `null` for the XSLT settings argument.

---
Adapted from [Microsoft and contributors](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/standard/data/xml/xslt-security-considerations.md). [CC BY 4.0; code MIT](/licenses/library-dotnet--docs.txt). Prompts, formatting, and selected wording adapted for Recall; source license applies to this material.

cards.front:
**XSLT Security Considerations / External Resources**

Explain External Resources in the context of XSLT Security Considerations.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

The XSLT language has features such as `xsl:import`, `xsl:include`, or the `document()` function, where the processor needs to resolve URI references. The `System.Xml.XmlResolver` class is used to resolve external resources. External resources may need to be resolved in the following two cases:

- When compiling a style sheet, the `System.Xml.XmlResolver` is used for `xsl:import` and `xsl:include` resolution.

- When executing the transformation, the `System.Xml.XmlResolver` is used to resolve the `document()` function.

  > The `document()` function is disabled by default on the `System.Xml.Xsl.XslCompiledTransform` class. This feature can be enabled by setting the `System.Xml.Xsl.XsltSettings.EnableDocumentFunction` property to `true` and passing the `System.Xml.Xsl.XsltSettings` object to the `System.Xml.Xsl.XslCompiledTransform.Load` method.

The `System.Xml.Xsl.XslCompiledTransform.Load` and `System.Xml.Xsl.XslCompiledTransform.Transform` methods each include overloads that accept an `System.Xml.XmlResolver` as one of its arguments. If an `System.Xml.XmlResolver` is not specified, a default `System.Xml.XmlUrlResolver` with no credentials is used.

cards.front:
**XSLT Security Considerations / External Resources / Guidelines**

Explain External Resources / Guidelines in the context of XSLT Security Considerations.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

Enable the `document()` function only when the style sheet comes from a trusted source.

The following list describes when you may want to specify an `System.Xml.XmlResolver` object:

- If the XSLT process needs to access a network resource that requires authentication, you can use an `System.Xml.XmlResolver` with the necessary credentials.

- If you want to restrict the resources that the XSLT process can access, you can use an `System.Xml.XmlSecureResolver` with the correct permission set. Use the `System.Xml.XmlSecureResolver` class if you need to open a resource that you do not control, or that is untrusted.

- If you want to customize behavior, you can implement your own `System.Xml.XmlResolver` class and use it to resolve resources.

- If you want to ensure that no external resources are accessed, you can specify `null` for the `System.Xml.XmlResolver` argument.

---

**Cross-platform cryptography / Authenticated encryption**

Explain Authenticated encryption in the context of Cross-platform cryptography.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

Authenticated encryption (AE) support is provided for AES-CCM, AES-GCM, and ChaCha20Poly1305 via the `System.Security.Cryptography.AesCcm`, `System.Security.Cryptography.AesGcm`, and `System.Security.Cryptography.ChaCha20Poly1305` classes, respectively.

Since authenticated encryption requires newer platform APIs to support the algorithm, support might not be present on all platforms. To detect at runtime whether the current platform supports the algorithm, you can use the `IsSupported` static property on the class for the algorithm.

| Cipher + Mode     | Windows                 | Linux          | macOS   | iOS, tvOS, MacCatalyst | Android       | Browser |
|-------------------|-------------------------|----------------|---------|------------------------|---------------|---------|
| AES-GCM           | ✔️                      | ✔️            | ✔️      | ⚠️                     | ✔️            | ❌      |
| AES-CCM           | ✔️                      | ✔️            | ❌      | ❌                     | ✔️            | ❌      |
| ChaCha20Poly1305  | Windows 10 Build 20142+ | OpenSSL 1.1.0+ | ✔️      | ⚠️                     | API Level 28+ | ❌      |

cards.front:
**Cross-platform cryptography / Authenticated encryption / AES-CCM keys, nonces, and tags**

Explain Authenticated encryption / AES-CCM keys, nonces, and tags in the context of Cross-platform cryptography.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

- Key Sizes

  AES-CCM works with 128, 192, and 256-bit keys.

- Nonce Sizes

  The `System.Security.Cryptography.AesCcm` class supports 56, 64, 72, 80, 88, 96, and 104-bit (7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13-byte) nonces.

- Tag Sizes

  The `System.Security.Cryptography.AesCcm` class supports creating or processing 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112, and 128-bit (4, 8, 10, 12, 14, and 16-byte) tags.

---

cards.front:
**Cross-platform cryptography / Authenticated encryption / AES-GCM keys, nonces, and tags**

Explain Authenticated encryption / AES-GCM keys, nonces, and tags in the context of Cross-platform cryptography.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

- Key Sizes

  AES-GCM works with 128, 192, and 256-bit keys.

- Nonce Sizes

  The `System.Security.Cryptography.AesGcm` class supports only 96-bit (12-byte) nonces.

- Tag Sizes

  On Windows and Linux, the `System.Security.Cryptography.AesGcm` class supports creating or processing 96, 104, 112, 120, and 128-bit (12, 13, 14, 15, and 16-byte) tags. On Apple platforms, the tag size is limited to 128-bit (16-byte) due to limitations of the CryptoKit framework.

cards.front:
**Cross-platform cryptography / Asymmetric cryptography / RSA / RSA on Windows**

Explain Asymmetric cryptography / RSA / RSA on Windows in the context of Cross-platform cryptography.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

- Windows CryptoAPI (CAPI) is used whenever `System.Security.Cryptography.RSACryptoServiceProvider` is used.
- Windows Cryptography API Next Generation (CNG) is used whenever `System.Security.Cryptography.RSACng` is used.
- The object returned by `System.Security.Cryptography.RSA.Create` is internally powered by Windows CNG. This use of Windows CNG is an implementation detail and is subject to change.
- The `System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates.RSACertificateExtensions.GetRSAPublicKey` extension method for `System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates.X509Certificate2` returns an `System.Security.Cryptography.RSACng` instance. This use of `System.Security.Cryptography.RSACng` is an implementation detail and is subject to change.
- The `System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates.RSACertificateExtensions.GetRSAPrivateKey` extension method for `System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates.X509Certificate2` currently prefers an `System.Security.Cryptography.RSACng` instance, but if `System.Security.Cryptography.RSACng` can't open the key, `System.Security.Cryptography.RSACryptoServiceProvider` will be attempted. The preferred provider is an implementation detail and is subject to change.

---

Explain Asymmetric cryptography / ECDSA / ECDSA Native Interop in the context of Cross-platform cryptography.

<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Explanation

.NET exposes types to allow programs to interoperate with the OS libraries that the .NET cryptography code uses. The types involved don't translate between platforms and should only be directly used when necessary.

| Type                                             | Windows | Linux | macOS | iOS, tvOS, MacCatalyst | Android |
|--------------------------------------------------|---------|-------|-------|------------------------|---------|
| `System.Security.Cryptography.ECDsaCng`     | ✔️      | ❌   | ❌    | ❌                     | ❌      |
| `System.Security.Cryptography.ECDsaOpenSsl` | ❌      | ✔️   | ❌\*  | ❌                     | ❌      |

\* On macOS, prior to .NET 10, `System.Security.Cryptography.ECDsaOpenSsl` worked if OpenSSL was installed and an appropriate libcrypto dylib could be found via dynamic library loading. This support was removed in .NET 10.
